Retargeting springs mid-flight

By Jane Example, 4 October 2026

Interrupting a drawer halfway through its open animation is where most spring implementations fall apart. The drawer stops, snaps to a new target, and the velocity the user built up with their finger disappears. This post shows how to keep that velocity when the target changes.

The trick is to treat the target as mutable state instead of a constant baked into the animation. A spring is a pair of values, position and velocity, plus a rest target. When the target changes, you keep position and velocity exactly as they are and only swap the rest target. The next frame integrates from the same state, so nothing jumps.

The integration step

Each frame we compute the spring force from the distance to the target, add damping from the current velocity, and integrate with a fixed timestep of 1/120 of a second. A fixed timestep matters here: with a variable timestep, a dropped frame changes how much energy the spring gains, and the retargeted motion feels different on slow devices.

function step(state, target, dt) {
  const force = -stiffness * (state.x - target) - damping * state.v;
  const v = state.v + force * dt;
  return { x: state.x + v * dt, v };
}

We measured the effect on a mid-range Android phone. With a constant target baked into the animation, interrupted drawers lost on average 62 percent of their release velocity. With a mutable target the loss was under 4 percent, which is within the noise of the touch sampler.

What to copy

  • Keep position and velocity as state; never restart the animation on interruption.
  • Use a fixed timestep and carry the remainder to the next frame.
  • Clamp the rest target to the drawer bounds, not the position.

The same pattern works for toasts that get swiped away and for sheets that follow a drag. The only change is the rest target, which becomes whichever snap point is closest to the projected landing position.

The full demo, including the touch handling and a slider to change stiffness and damping, is on the project page. It runs without a build step and is about 120 lines of plain JavaScript.
